summary: The Earth Sustainability Initiative (ESI) is a trend detective with one mission: helping keep Earth habitable for future generations. Using NASA satellite and model data from 2002 to 2025, it looks at air temperature, ground temperature, rainfall and vegetation in 11 of the world’s biggest cities. For each one, it shows whether things are changing, how fast, and whether the change is real or just noise. It also shows how long a city would take to reach a known habitability threshold if its current trend simply carried on. ESI doesn’t predict the future. It gives people clear, open evidence to explore, so they can make their own decisions and predictions about the planet we share.
details:
What it does. ESI is a monitoring tool. It tracks the things Earth’s habitability depends on and shows how they are changing in the 11 biggest cities (the top 10 by the UN’s 2025 city rankings, plus Lagos). For each city, it covers air temperature, daytime and night-time ground temperature, rainfall and vegetation, using NASA data from 2002 to 2025.

How it works. We remove the normal seasonal ups and downs, then look at how each year compares with the long-term average. A statistical test (Mann-Kendall) tells us whether a trend is real or could be chance, and Sen’s slope gives its speed per decade. Each city also gets a “habitability pressure” score. Half comes from how strong the trends are, and half from how close conditions are to recognized thresholds. We also show a what-if: how many years it would take to reach a threshold if the current trend continued, capped at 100 years. This is not a forecast. It is a way to see which trends deserve attention.

What we found. Eight of the 11 cities show significant air-temperature warming, and five show significant night-time ground warming. Only Guangzhou and Shanghai show a significant rainfall change, and both are getting wetter. No city reaches the “high” pressure band, and Shanghai ranks highest, in the moderate band. We also flag what we can’t explain. New Delhi’s air-temperature cooling is unresolved, and we make no claim about its cause.

Why it matters. People can only act on what they can see. ESI turns 24 years of open NASA data into something anyone can explore, with plain-language definitions, no login and full citations. The people who use it make the decisions and predictions, and ESI gives them the evidence.

How we built it. The analysis is in Python (pandas, NumPy and pymannkendall), served by a FastAPI backend. The front end is vanilla TypeScript built with Vite, with an interactive globe drawn using d3-geo and world-atlas. The published site runs entirely from pre-computed files, so it needs no server. We used NASA’s MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, AIRS and MODIS NDVI (through AppEEARS) data.

How it fits in. Tools already exist for mapping urban heat, mostly for one city, one country or one neighborhood at a time. ESI takes a wider view. It follows temperature, rainfall and vegetation together across the world’s biggest cities, tests whether each trend is real, and says plainly when something can’t be explained. It is a starting point, built to grow with more cities and indicators.
